Text: Pipecat is the next step after “chatbot with a microphone.”

Most people still build voice agents like this:

Record audio.
Send it to speech-to-text.
Pass text to an LLM.
Send the answer to text-to-speech.
Glue it together.
Pray the latency feels human.

This repo shows the next step:

You stop treating voice as an add-on.

You build the whole real-time conversation pipeline.

Pipecat is an open-source Python framework for building voice and multimodal AI agents. It helps orchestrate audio, video, AI services, transports, and conversation logic in one pipeline. ([GitHub][1])

Inside:

→ Real-time voice agents
→ Multimodal agents
→ Audio and video pipelines
→ Streaming conversation handling
→ WebSocket and WebRTC transports
→ Pluggable STT, LLM, and TTS services
→ Composable pipeline components
→ Low-latency interaction
→ Client SDKs for web and mobile
→ Examples for assistants, support bots, companions, and guided flows

The wild part is the shift in thinking.

A voice agent is not just a chatbot that speaks.

It needs turn-taking.
Interruptions.
Streaming.
Transport.
Latency control.
Audio handling.
Conversation state.
Tool calls.
Fallbacks.
Human-like timing.

That is why most voice demos feel impressive for 30 seconds and then break the moment a real person talks over them.

Pipecat gives builders the framework layer underneath the voice agent.

This is what voice AI looks like when it stops being a demo script and starts becoming real-time software.
